claims.claim: In a many-to-many relationship, a row in one table can match many rows in another table, and a row in the other table can match many rows in the first — the 'many' runs in both directions.
Students and courses is the canonical many-to-many example: a student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students.
A many-to-many relationship cannot be represented with a single foreign key; an additional table is required to join the two sides.
The bridge (join) table stores one row per pairing; each row holds a pair of identifying values, one pointing to a row on each side of the relationship.
A many-to-many relationship reads in two directions: a student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students — both readings are answered by the same bridge table.
In a one-to-many relationship, each value in one table matches only one value in another; many-to-many is the case where the 'many' applies on both sides.
A foreign key is a column in one table whose values refer to the primary key of another table, establishing a link between the two tables — a single value pointing at a single row.

Many-to-many is the least obvious relationship pattern because it demands a third table that holds no facts of its own, and the most powerful because it models two-sided real-world pairings such as students and courses or customers and accounts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What to call the third table that records a many-to-many relationship.
positions: Microsoft's EF Core documentation calls it the join entity type, which maps to a join table in a relational database.
Microsoft's Power BI documentation calls it a bridging table that connects the two main tables by listing all valid combinations of their keys.
Textbooks and tutorials commonly use the term junction table for the same structure.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The names describe the same mechanism. The lesson leads with 'bridge table' as the plain-language term and notes 'join table' as the equivalent term used in database documentation.
